## Tutorial 1: Networks on maps

### 1.1 A spatial network dataset

Use a small dataset with real coordinates — e.g. NZ regional centres
(toy example below), or a dataset from earlier in the course (the
choropleth/mapping weeks may already have a suitable `sf` object you
can reuse).

```{r}
cities <- data.frame(
  name = c("Auckland", "Wellington", "Christchurch", "Hamilton",
           "Dunedin", "Tauranga", "Palmerston North"),
  lon  = c(174.76, 174.78, 172.64, 175.28, 170.50, 176.17, 175.61),
  lat  = c(-36.85, -41.29, -43.53, -37.78, -45.87, -37.69, -40.36),
  population = c(1657000, 215100, 396700, 184900, 134600, 158300, 89300)
)
population <- setNames(cities$population, cities$name)

# A simple set of edges (e.g. main connections between centres)
edges <- data.frame(
  from = c("Auckland","Auckland","Hamilton","Wellington","Wellington","Tauranga"),
  to   = c("Wellington","Hamilton","Tauranga","Christchurch","Palmerston North","Christchurch")
)

g <- tbl_graph(nodes = cities, edges = edges, directed = FALSE)
```

### 1.2 Plotting with manual layout

```{r}
ggraph(g, layout = "manual", x = cities$lon, y = cities$lat) +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.5, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_node_point(aes(size = population), colour = "darkred") +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), repel = TRUE, size = 3) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 10) +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 1.4) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "A spatial network of NZ centres",
       x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude", size = "Population")
```

**Exercise 1.1** - Find an `sf` polygon dataset of NZ regions (e.g.
`rnaturalearth`, or one reused from the choropleth weeks). Plot it with
`geom_sf()` as a background layer, then overlay the network from above.
Check the CRS of both layers (`st_crs()`). If they differ, use
`st_transform()` so they align.

### 1.3 Edge width as flow strength

**Exercise 1.2** - Add an edge attribute (e.g. invent a "flow" value,
or compute one as `pmin(population[from], population[to])`), and map
it to `geom_edge_link(aes(width = flow))`. Use `scale_edge_width()` to
control the range. Discuss: at what point would this network have too
many edges for width-encoding to remain readable, and what would you
do instead (refer back to Week 7's hairball discussion)?

## Tutorial 2: Visualising change over time

### 2.1 A network that grows over time

```{r}
nodes <- data.frame(name = LETTERS[1:8])

all_edges <- data.frame(
  from = c("A","A","B","C","D","A","E","F","G","B"),
  to   = c("B","C","C","D","E","F","F","G","H","H"),
  time = c(1,1,1,2,2,2,3,3,3,4)
)
```

### 2.2 Small multiples (snapshots)

```{r}
make_snapshot <- function(t) {
  edges_t <- all_edges |> filter(time <= t)
  g_t <- tbl_graph(nodes = nodes, edges = edges_t, directed = FALSE)
  ggraph(g_t, layout = "fr") +
    geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_node_point(size = 3) +
    geom_node_text(aes(label = name), repel = TRUE, size = 3) +
    theme_void() +
    labs(title = paste("t =", t))
}

# NOTE: each call to ggraph(layout = "fr") re-runs the layout algorithm,
# so node positions may move between panels. See Exercise 2.1.
wrap_plots(lapply(1:4, make_snapshot), nrow = 1)
```

**Exercise 2.1** - The snapshots above likely show nodes "jumping
around" between panels, because each panel recomputes its own
force-directed layout. Fix this by computing **one** layout using the
*final* (most complete) network, extracting node coordinates
(`create_layout()`), and reusing those fixed coordinates
(`layout = "manual", x = ..., y = ...`) for every snapshot. Regenerate
the small multiples. How does this change your interpretation of
"network growth" across panels?

### 2.3 Animation (optional, time permitting)

**Exercise 2.2 (optional)** - If `gganimate` is available, animate the
snapshots from 2.2 (fixed layout) as a `transition_states()` animation.
Compare the animated version to the small-multiples version: which
makes it easier to (a) see the *final* network structure, (b) see *when*
a particular edge was added? Relate this back to the Week 5
spaghetti-vs-small-multiples discussion: what's the temporal analogue
of "overplotting" here?

## Tutorial 3 (double session): Capstone simulated spread with uncertainty

### Short session: A simple epidemic-on-network simulation

We will use a small fixed network and a very simple stochastic SIR-type
process: at each time step, each infected node infects each susceptible
neighbour independently with probability `p_infect` (or `beta` in the lectures), 
and each infected node recovers with probability `p_recover` (or `gamma` in the 
lectures).

```{r}
set.seed(1)

# A moderately sized random network
n_nodes <- 30
g_sim <- play_erdos_renyi(n_nodes, p = 0.08, directed = FALSE) |>
  mutate(name = as.character(1:n_nodes))

adj <- as.matrix(igraph::as_adjacency_matrix(g_sim))

simulate_sir <- function(adj, p_infect = 0.15, p_recover = 0.1,
                          n_steps = 30, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  n <- nrow(adj)
  status <- rep("S", n)
  status[sample(1:n, 1)] <- "I"  # one initial infection

  history <- matrix(NA_character_, nrow = n_steps, ncol = n)
  history[1, ] <- status

  for (t in 2:n_steps) {
    infected <- which(status == "I")
    susceptible <- which(status == "S")

    new_infections <- c()
    for (s in susceptible) {
      neighbours <- which(adj[s, ] == 1)
      n_infected_neighbours <- sum(neighbours %in% infected)
      if (n_infected_neighbours > 0) {
        prob_escape <- (1 - p_infect)^n_infected_neighbours
        if (runif(1) > prob_escape) new_infections <- c(new_infections, s)
      }
    }

    recoveries <- infected[runif(length(infected)) < p_recover]

    status[new_infections] <- "I"
    status[recoveries] <- "R"
    history[t, ] <- status
  }

  history
}

# One realisation
hist1 <- simulate_sir(adj, seed = 1)
```

**Exercise 3.1** - Compute, for `hist1`, the number of S/I/R individuals
at each time step (e.g. `apply(hist1, 1, table)`). Plot these three
counts over time as a simple line plot (three lines, one per
compartment). This is the "compartment trajectory" idiom from Lecture
2, and structurally identical to a Week 5 single-realisation plot.

### Long session (after break)

#### Panel A: Network snapshot

**Exercise 3.2** - Choose a time point `t` partway through the
epidemic (e.g. where I is near its peak in `hist1`). Build a
`tbl_graph` from `g_sim`, add a `status` node attribute from
`hist1[t, ]`, and plot with `geom_node_point(aes(colour = status))`
using a clear S/I/R colour scheme (e.g. grey/red/blue). This is Panel A
of your capstone figure.

#### Panel B: Multiple runs with uncertainty ribbon

```{r}
n_sims <- 100
n_steps <- 30

results <- lapply(1:n_sims, function(i) {
  h <- simulate_sir(adj, seed = i, n_steps = n_steps)
  data.frame(
    sim = i,
    time = 1:n_steps,
    n_infected = rowSums(h == "I")
  )
})
results <- bind_rows(results)
```

**Exercise 3.3** - Using `results`, build a ribbon plot of `n_infected`
over time (median + 50%/90% bands across the 100 simulations). This is
*exactly* the Week 5/6 ribbon code, applied to a new variable. This is
Panel B of your capstone figure.

#### Panel C: Spatial view (optional, if coordinates available)

**Exercise 3.4 (optional)** - If you have or can assign coordinates to
the 30 nodes (e.g. random points within a region, or real locations if
relevant to your data), reuse Tutorial 1's `layout = "manual"` approach
to plot Panel A's network snapshot on a map instead of an abstract
layout.

#### Assembling the capstone figure

**Final task** - Combine Panels A and B (and C if completed) into a
single multi-panel figure using `patchwork`. Add:

- A overall title and panel labels (e.g. `plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")`)
- A short caption stating the simulation parameters (`p_infect`,
  `p_recover`, network size, number of simulation runs, and **seeds
  used**); this is the reproducibility record for a stochastic figure

Accompany the figure with a written rationale (~250 words) addressing:

- Which week's material does each panel draw on? Be explicit (e.g.
  "Panel B uses the ribbon technique from Week 5/6, applied to...")
- What does the multi-panel figure communicate that no single panel
  could on its own?
- What design choices (colour, layout, theme) did you make to keep the
  panels visually consistent with each other and with the course's
  established conventions?
- Reference at least two course readings spanning at least two
  different weeks' topics (e.g. one network reference, one
  uncertainty/visualisation reference).

This figure and write-up form the course's capstone deliverable,
integrating simulation (Week 5), uncertainty (Week 6), network
visualisation (Week 7), and spatial/dynamic network visualisation
(Week 8).
